title: Finance and Growth
summary: Use the simple and compound growth formulae to solve problems on interest, hire purchase, inflation, population growth and exchange rates.

notes.text: Why finance matters

Whether you are saving for a matric dance outfit, buying a cellphone on credit or planning to study at university, you will deal with **interest**. Banks pay you interest when you save and charge you interest when you borrow. In this topic you learn the two basic ways in which money grows (simple and compound growth) and apply them to hire purchase, inflation, population growth and exchange rates.
The amount of money originally invested or borrowed (the starting amount).
The final amount after interest has been added: principal plus all the interest.
The percentage of the principal earned or charged per period, written as a **decimal** in formulae. For example $8\%$ per annum (p.a., per year) gives $i = 0{,}08$.
The number of periods (usually years) for which the money is invested or borrowed.

notes.label: Remember
notes.text: Convert percentages to decimals by dividing by 100: $12\% = 0{,}12$, $7{,}5\% = 0{,}075$, $0{,}5\% = 0{,}005$. If time is given in months, convert it to years for an annual rate: $18$ months $= 1{,}5$ years.
Simple interest

With **simple interest**, interest is calculated **only on the original principal**. The same amount of interest is added every year, so the investment grows in a straight line (linear growth). Each year the interest is $P \times i$, so after $n$ years the total interest is $I = Pin$.

notes.title: Worked example 1: calculating A (simple interest)
notes.problem: Naledi invests R8 000 at $7{,}5\%$ p.a. simple interest for 4 years. Calculate the accumulated amount and the total interest earned.

notes.text: Solving for P, i and n with simple interest
Substitute the values you know into $A = P(1 + in)$ and solve the resulting linear equation. Do not round in the middle of your working.

notes.problem: R5 000 grows to R6 800 in 3 years at a simple interest rate. Determine the annual interest rate.

notes.title: Worked example 3: finding the time period
notes.problem: How many years will it take R12 000 to grow to R17 400 at $9\%$ p.a. simple interest?

notes.title: Worked example 4: finding the principal
notes.problem: What amount must be invested at $6\%$ p.a. simple interest to grow to R9 750 after 5 years?

notes.text: Compound interest

With **compound interest**, the interest earned each period is added to the balance, and the next period's interest is calculated on this new, larger balance. You earn **interest on interest**. Each year the balance is multiplied by $(1 + i)$, so after $n$ years it has been multiplied by $(1 + i)^n$. This is exponential growth, linking to the exponential graph you studied in Term 2.

notes.title: Worked example 5: calculating A (compound interest)
notes.problem: Naledi invests R8 000 at $7{,}5\%$ p.a. compounded annually for 4 years. Calculate the accumulated amount and compare it with simple interest (Worked example 1).
steps: Compound interest gives $10\,683{,}75 - 10\,400 = \text{R}283{,}75$ more than simple interest.

notes.caption: R10 000 invested at 10% p.a.: simple versus compound growth

notes.text: Notice that after year 1 the two balances are equal, but then compound interest pulls ahead. Simple interest adds a constant R1 000 each year (a linear pattern), while compound interest adds more each year because each year's interest is $10\%$ of a bigger balance (an exponential pattern). Over long periods the difference becomes very large.

notes.text: Compounding more than once a year

Interest is often added more than once a year. If the annual rate is $i$ and interest is compounded $m$ times per year, then each period the rate is $\dfrac{i}{m}$, and over $n$ years there are $n \times m$ periods.

notes.caption: Compound interest with m compounding periods per year

notes.title: Worked example 6: quarterly compounding
notes.problem: Sibusiso invests R20 000 at $8\%$ p.a. compounded quarterly for 3 years. Calculate the value of the investment after 3 years.
steps: Rate per quarter: $\dfrac{0{,}08}{4} = 0{,}02$. Number of quarters: $3 \times 4 = 12$.

notes.label: Common mistake
notes.text: If you change the rate to $\frac{i}{m}$ you **must** also change the exponent to $n \times m$. Writing $20\,000(1{,}02)^3$ is wrong: it uses a quarterly rate for only 3 quarters.
For the same annual rate, more frequent compounding gives slightly more money, because interest starts earning interest sooner.
Solving for P and i with compound interest

notes.title: Worked example 7: finding the principal (present value)
notes.problem: How much must Aisha invest now at $9\%$ p.a. compounded annually so that she has R50 000 in 6 years' time for university fees?

notes.title: Worked example 8: finding the compound interest rate
notes.problem: An investment of R15 000 grew to R22 000 in 5 years, with interest compounded annually. Calculate the annual interest rate, correct to two decimal places.
steps: Take the fifth root of both sides: $1 + i = \sqrt[5]{\dfrac{22\,000}{15\,000}} = \left(\dfrac{22\,000}{15\,000}\right)^{\frac{1}{5}} = 1{,}079608\ldots$

notes.label: Exam tip
notes.text: In Grade 10 you solve for $n$ only with **simple** interest. Finding $n$ in $A = P(1 + i)^n$ requires logarithms, which you will learn in Grade 12.
Hire purchase

**Hire purchase (HP)** is a way of buying an item (such as furniture, a fridge or a laptop) and paying for it over time. You pay a **deposit** up front and borrow the rest. The store charges **simple interest** on the amount owing for the whole period, and you repay the loan plus interest in equal **monthly instalments**. You only own the item once the final payment has been made.

items: Amount to be repaid $A = P(1 + in)$.
Monthly instalment $= \dfrac{A}{\text{number of months}}$ (add any monthly insurance).
Total cost $=$ deposit $+$ all instalments (including insurance).

notes.title: Worked example 9: hire purchase
notes.problem: Thandi buys a fridge with a cash price of R9 600 on hire purchase. She pays a $10\%$ deposit and the balance is financed over 2 years at $18\%$ p.a. simple interest. Calculate (a) the monthly instalment and (b) the total cost of the fridge.
notes.answer: (a) R489,60 per month  (b) R12 710,40, which is R3 110,40 more than the cash price

notes.title: Worked example 10: hire purchase with insurance
notes.problem: A laptop costs R12 000 cash. Jaco pays a deposit of R1 500 and finances the rest over 3 years at $15\%$ p.a. simple interest. The store adds compulsory insurance of R45 per month. Calculate his monthly payment and the total amount he pays.
notes.answer: R467,92 per month; about R18 345 in total (R18 345,12 if you multiply the rounded payment by 36)

notes.label: Common mistake
notes.text: Interest on hire purchase is charged on the amount **after** the deposit, not on the cash price. Also remember that the number of instalments is in **months** ($n$ years $= 12n$ months), while $n$ in the formula is in **years** for an annual rate.
Inflation
The general increase in the prices of goods and services over time. In South Africa it is measured by Stats SA using the Consumer Price Index (CPI) and is given as an annual percentage.

Inflation works like compound interest: each year prices increase by a percentage of the **previous year's** price. Use $A = P(1 + i)^n$, where $P$ is today's price, $i$ is the annual inflation rate and $A$ is the future price. To find a price in the past, solve for $P$.

notes.title: Worked example 11: future price
notes.problem: A loaf of bread costs R18,50. If the average inflation rate is $5{,}5\%$ p.a., what will it cost in 4 years' time?

notes.title: Worked example 12: price in the past
notes.problem: A small car costs R320 000 today. If inflation averaged $5\%$ p.a. over the last 4 years, what did a similar car cost 4 years ago?

notes.text: Population growth

Populations of people, animals or bacteria often grow by a fixed percentage each year, which is compound growth. Use $A = P(1 + i)^n$ with $P$ the current population and $A$ the future population. Round to a **whole number** because you cannot have part of a person.

notes.title: Worked example 13: population of a town
notes.problem: A town in Limpopo has 45 000 residents and the population grows at $2{,}3\%$ per year. Estimate the population in 10 years' time.

notes.text: Exchange rates
The price of one currency in terms of another, for example US\$1 $=$ R18,25 means that one United States dollar costs R18,25.

items: **Foreign currency to rand:** multiply by the rate. US\$240 at R18,25 per dollar costs $240 \times 18{,}25 = \text{R}4\,380$.
**Rand to foreign currency:** divide by the rate. R5 000 at R19,80 per euro buys $5\,000 \div 19{,}80 = 252{,}53$, that is €252,53 (rounded to the nearest cent).

notes.label: Exam tip
notes.text: Check that your answer makes sense. If R1 is worth much less than one unit of the foreign currency, you will get **fewer** foreign units than rand when you convert, and **more** rand than foreign units when you convert back.

Exchange rates change (fluctuate) daily because of supply and demand, interest rates, political events and commodity prices. When you need **more** rand to buy one dollar (for example the rate moves from R17,50 to R18,90), the rand has **weakened** (depreciated). When you need **fewer** rand, the rand has **strengthened** (appreciated).

notes.caption: Effects of a fluctuating rand
rows: SA is more expensive for them

notes.title: Worked example 14: the effect of a weaker rand
notes.problem: A cellphone costs US\$1 200 overseas. The exchange rate changes from R17,50 to R18,90 per US dollar. By how much does the rand price increase?
notes.answer: The phone costs R1 680 more because the rand weakened.

notes.text: Summary

items: Simple interest: $A = P(1 + in)$; interest on the principal only; linear growth.
Compound interest: $A = P(1 + i)^n$; interest on interest; exponential growth.
Write rates as decimals; $n$ is in years for an annual rate.
Compounding $m$ times per year: use $\frac{i}{m}$ as the rate and $n \times m$ as the number of periods.
You can solve for $A$, $P$ and $i$ in both formulae, and for $n$ in the simple interest formula.
Hire purchase: simple interest on (cash price $-$ deposit); instalment $= A \div$ number of months; total cost $=$ deposit $+$ all instalments.
Inflation and population growth use the compound growth formula; round population answers to whole numbers.
Exchange rates: foreign to rand, multiply; rand to foreign, divide. A weaker rand makes imports and overseas travel more expensive.
Do not round until the final answer; give money to the nearest cent.

questions.prompt: In the formula $A = P(1 + in)$, what does $n$ represent?
questions.explanation: $P$ is the principal, $i$ the interest rate as a decimal, $n$ the number of periods and $A$ the accumulated amount.

questions.prompt: With compound interest, interest is earned on the principal and on interest already earned.
questions.explanation: This is what makes compound interest grow faster than simple interest: you earn interest on interest.

questions.prompt: In hire purchase, interest is usually calculated as compound interest on the full cash price.
questions.explanation: Hire purchase uses simple interest, and it is charged on the amount owing after the deposit has been paid, not on the full cash price.

questions.prompt: R6 000 is invested at $8\%$ p.a. simple interest for 5 years. Calculate the accumulated amount in rand.
R6 000 is invested at $8\%$ p.a. compounded annually for 5 years. Calculate the accumulated amount, correct to the nearest cent.
questions.explanation: $A = 6\,000(1{,}08)^5 = 8\,815{,}968\ldots \approx \text{R}8\,815{,}97$. That is R415,97 more than simple interest in the previous question.

questions.prompt: R10 000 is invested for 4 years at $9\%$ p.a. compounded monthly. Which expression gives the accumulated amount?
questions.explanation: Monthly compounding: rate per month $= \frac{0{,}09}{12}$ and number of months $= 4 \times 12 = 48$. Both the rate and the exponent must change.

questions.prompt: Match each compounding frequency with the number of times interest is added per year.
questions.explanation: A year has 2 halves, 4 quarters and 12 months.

questions.prompt: R4 500 grows to R5 940 in 4 years at simple interest. Calculate the annual interest rate as a percentage.
The exchange rate is US\$1 $=$ R18,40. How many rand does a pair of sneakers costing US\$350 cost?
The rand/dollar exchange rate changes from R18,00 to R19,00 per US dollar. Which statement is correct?
options: The rand has weakened, so imported goods become more expensive.
The rand has strengthened, so imported goods become cheaper.
The rand has weakened, so overseas holidays become cheaper for South Africans.
The rand has strengthened, so exporters earn more rand per sale.
questions.explanation: More rand are now needed to buy one dollar, so the rand has weakened. Anything priced in dollars (imports, overseas travel) now costs more in rand.

questions.prompt: How many years will it take for R7 000 to grow to R10 360 at $6\%$ p.a. simple interest?
How much must be invested now at $10\%$ p.a. compounded half-yearly to have R40 000 in 4 years' time? Give your answer correct to the nearest cent.
questions.explanation: Rate per half-year $= 0{,}05$, number of half-years $= 8$. $P = \dfrac{40\,000}{(1{,}05)^8} = 27\,073{,}574\ldots \approx \text{R}27\,073{,}57$.
